If you only remember one thing: Anthropic's Dario Amodei is dining with Trump at the White House tonight, despite months of open conflict over A I regulation. It's a signal moment for where Washington's A I rules go next.

Section one, A I developments and model news.
Anthropic C E O Dario Amodei is set to have dinner with President Trump at the White House, after weeks of public tension. Amodei has been one of the loudest voices calling for A I safety regulation, putting him at odds with an administration that wants the U S to, quote, not slow down, end quote, on A I. He also got the Saturday Night Live treatment this week, a sign of how central he's become to the A I conversation. Separately, Meta's new A I assistant, Muse, is still fighting to earn user trust. And Google is testing A I powered shopping through Gemini, in partnership with Flipkart in India. From your Reads: your China A I Weekly digest reports the U S and China have opened a new A I dialogue, Alibaba is targeting twenty gigawatts of global data center capacity, and Deep Seek is reportedly nearing a seven point five billion dollar funding round.
Why it matters: the Amodei-Trump dinner is a real time test of whether Silicon Valley's safety advocates can find common ground with an administration pushing full speed ahead.

Section two, A I ethics and policy.
The Pentagon wants thirty million dollars to build an A I powered lie detector called Polygraph Plus, for staff vetting. Researchers are already warning about reliability. The E U is working through how its new KIDS Act, aimed at child protection online, fits into its broader digital rulebook. And Tech Policy Press, from your Reads, flagged a split at the U N this week: global leaders are clashing over whether A I governance should be set in Washington, or through a U N style multilateral process.
Why it matters: the fight over who writes A I's rules, one government or a global table, is quietly being decided right now.

Section three, tech geopolitics.
The U S, China A I dialogue mentioned earlier comes as China is reportedly considering tighter export controls of its own, on A I models and chips, a mirror move to Washington's existing restrictions. Meanwhile, Europe is grappling with what analysts call a digital sovereignty funding gap: big ambitions to reduce dependence on U S and Chinese tech, without the budget to match.
Why it matters: the chip and A I model chess match between Washington and Beijing is entering a new phase, and Europe risks being a spectator in its own backyard.

Section four, technology for good.
Rest of World reports humanitarian aid groups are turning to A I, as refugee and crisis caseloads outpace their capacity. The I R C's Signpost project is one example of A I helping triage and route assistance faster. Separately, A I dominated conversation at Climate Week, as groups debate whether the technology is a net help, or a new energy drain on climate goals.
Why it matters: while Silicon Valley debates trust and dinner invitations, aid groups are quietly proving what useful A I deployment looks like on the ground.

Section five, media industry.
Four oh four Media's latest podcast covers Open A I effectively admitting that A I generated content is degrading the quality of the internet, as A I spam increasingly floods legitimate platforms.
Why it matters: for anyone in comms, this is the slow motion story. Trust in what's real online keeps eroding, and now it's the companies building the A I tools saying so themselves.

Also in your Reads: Reframing Climate Change shared a video of a NYC Climate Week talk, plus a piece on saving America's roadless forests. Nothing urgent, just flagged so it's not lost.

Quick thread wrap up: today's throughline is trust and rules. Who gets to write them, who's testing the room, and who's quietly doing the real work while the debate rages.

That's your briefing for today. Talk to you tomorrow.
